questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040724/assets/0c46972a3968d7110cb08d4b16bfff9267e49b102cf005cdbb21a3630d15c49d.png)

Consider the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal radius $7$ and vertical radius $2,$ as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$  traverse the ellipse once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(7,0)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=b\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the ellipse is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(a,0).$

In our case, $a=7$ and $b=2.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the ellipse are

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040724/assets/5b344621d5500d3253295c970b0a7557b80f4d2cbfa66c17ba6f8868c1424c08.png)

The quarter-ellipse above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=b\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, $a=2$ and $b=3.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the *full* ellipse are

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-ellipse, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the elipse and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040724/assets/9e236591e21403bb739dafa68a665c8a10eed0e9e8ac104e7b39431f02329c17.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}]$, we get the quarter-ellipse.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-ellipse are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}].
$$

questions.problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the ellipse

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{5} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 
Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25}=1.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{4} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 
Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}=1.
$$

questions.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the ellipse

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1 \\ \frac{x+1}{4} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{16} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1 \\ y-1 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ (y-1)^{2} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{16}+(y-1)^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{16}+(y-1)^{2}=1.
$$

The Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by the parametric equations

questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\sqrt{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{4\sqrt{6}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(4\sqrt{6})^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{96} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{5\sqrt{2}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{(5\sqrt{2})^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{50} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{96}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{50}={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{96}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{50}=1.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: The Parametric Equations of an Ellipse Centered at the Origin
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal radius $3$ and vertical radius $1,$ as shown below. Which set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi),$  traverse the ellipse once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(3,0)?$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040724/assets/5d791b30556f41973c8f1a9b8702744afae72458d0ce285de2b7ef8fa19d720a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x= a\cos\theta,\quad y=b\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

Under this parametrization, the ellipse is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(a,0).$

In our case, $a=3$ and $b=1.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the ellipse are

$$
x= 3\cos\theta,\quad y=\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: The Parametric Equations of an Ellipse Centered at a General Point
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the ellipse centered at $(1,-2)$ with horizontal radius $6$ and vertical radius $4,$ as shown below. Which set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi),$ traverse the ellipse once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(7,-2)?$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040724/assets/4724f0bcc1499be95dc8a28584511ecdb86d078b8205ad81a6e836ba1bdd261c.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the point $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x= a\cos\theta+h,\quad y=b\sin\theta+k, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

Under this parametrization, the ellipse is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(h+a,k).$

In our case, the ellipse is centered at the point $(1,-2),$ $a=6$ and $b=4.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the ellipse are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta+1,\quad y=4\sin\theta-2,\quad \theta\in [0,2\pi).
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The semi-ellipse below is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x = 5\cos\theta, \qquad y = 4\sin\theta.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040724/assets/6ca367eb7dc7cbd8205cbd85ad6d2503f957defd3f9a10e7b510759f41e0c778.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x= a\cos\theta,\quad y=b\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

In our case, $a=5$ and $b=4.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the *full* ellipse are

$$
x= 5\cos\theta,\quad y=4\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a semi-ellipse, we associate the parameter $\theta$ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the ellipse and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040724/assets/a64898381b2cf50c71a79a3dbcf02b9a83f320b8c2d1ba542b3beecc05e17625.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta$ to $\left[0, \pi\right],$ we get the semi-ellipse.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the semi-ellipse are 

$$
x= 5\cos\theta,\quad y=4\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in\left[0, \pi\right].
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: The Cartesian Equation of an Ellipse
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse

$$
x= 4\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta - 1, \quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta.$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{4} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y+1}{2} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+1)^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 
Adding the two equations and using $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{(y+1)^2}{4} = 1.
$$
